en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 148, the Chachakkasutta (The Discourse on the Six Sets of Six) Thus have I heard: [the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these six internal sense bases. What six? The eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base. These, bhikkhus, are the six internal sense bases. [And so forth, repeating the same formula for each of the six external sense bases, the six classes of consciousness, the six classes of contact, the six classes of feeling, the six classes of craving, and the six classes of elements. “Bhikkhus, there are these six internal sense bases... six external sense bases... six classes of consciousness... six classes of contact... six classes of feeling...

six classes of craving... six classes of elements. These, bhikkhus, are the six sets of six. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have not fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases, the six external sense bases, the six classes of consciousness, the six classes of contact, the six classes of feeling, the six classes of craving, and the six classes of elements. It is for this reason that some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements. It is for this reason that some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, another bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have not developed, cultivated, and made much of the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements. It is for this reason that some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have developed, cultivated, and made much of the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements. It is for this reason that some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have not abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements. It is for this reason that some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements. It is for this reason that some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, still another bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have not fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements, and they have not developed, cultivated, and made much of them, and they have not abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for them. It is for this reason that some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements; they have developed, cultivated, and made much of them; and they have abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for them. It is for this reason that some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have not fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements, and they have not developed, cultivated, and made much of them, and they have not abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for them, and they have not even attained the path leading to the complete destruction of suffering. It is for this reason that some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements; they have developed, cultivated, and made much of them; they have abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for them; and they have attained the path leading to the complete destruction of suffering. It is for this reason that some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, still another bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have not fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements, and they have not developed, cultivated, and made much of them, and they have not abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for them, and they have not even attained the path leading to the complete destruction of suffering, and they have not even entered upon the way leading to the complete destruction of suffering. It is for this reason that some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements; they have developed, cultivated, and made much of them; they have abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for them;

they have attained the path leading to the complete destruction of suffering; and they have entered upon the way leading to the complete destruction of suffering. It is for this reason that some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have not fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements, and they have not developed, cultivated, and made much of them, and they have not abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for them, and they have not even attained the path leading to the complete destruction of suffering, and they have not even entered upon the way leading to the complete destruction of suffering, and they have not even reached the destination of those who have reached the destination. It is for this reason that some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life? “Bhikkhu, it is because they have fully understood, as they really are, the six internal sense bases... the six classes of elements; they have developed, cultivated, and made much of them; they have abandoned, dispelled, and eradicated the underlying tendency toward lust for them; they have attained the path leading to the complete destruction of suffering; they have entered upon the way
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“I shall teach you the Dhamma, bhikkhus, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its own meaning and phrasing; I shall reveal the holy life, entirely complete and pure, namely:”
“There are six sets of six.
Listen to them and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this: “Six internal sense bases are to be understood; six external sense bases are to be understood; six groups of consciousness are to be understood; six groups of contact are to be understood; six groups of feeling are to be understood; six groups of craving are to be understood.
‘Six internal sense bases are to be understood’—”
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
The eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base.
“The six internal bases are to be understood”—thus it was said.
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
This is the first hexad:
“The six external sense bases are to be understood.”
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
The base of visible forms, the base of sounds, the base of odors, the base of flavors, the base of tangibles, and the base of mental phenomena.
“The six external bases are to be understood”—this is what was said.
Thus, that which was said, this was said with reference to this.
This is the second hexad:
"The six classes of consciousness are to be understood."
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;
dependent upon the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises.
Dependent on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises;
dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises;
dependent on the body and tangible objects, body-consciousness arises.
Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises.
Regarding that which was said— "The six classes of consciousness are to be understood"— this is what it refers to.
This is the third set of six.
“‘The six classes of contact should be understood’—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?”
Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact.
Dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact.
Dependent on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact.
Dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact.
Dependent on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact.
Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact.
‘The six bodies of contact should be understood’—
this is what was said, and it is in reference to this that it was said.
This is the fourth set of six.
‘The six classes of feeling are to be understood’—so it was said.
With reference to what was this said?
Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling [arises].
Dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises.
Dependent on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises.
Dependent on the tongue and flavors, tongue-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises.
Dependent on the body and tangible objects, body-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling.
Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling.
“The six groups of feeling are to be understood”—thus it was said.
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
This is the fifth set of six.
“The six classes of craving should be understood.”
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving.
Dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises... [and so on].
Dependent on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises;
dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises;
dependent on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises.
“Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving.
Regarding this, it was said: “The six classes of craving should be understood”—this is what was said with reference to this.
This is the sixth set of six.
If anyone were to say, "The eye is the self," that is not tenable.
For the arising and the passing away of the eye are both discerned.
But for one in whom both arising and passing away are discerned, it occurs to them: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, it is not tenable for anyone to say, "The eye is the self."
Thus, the eye is not-self.
If anyone were to say, "Forms are self," that is not tenable;
for the arising and the passing away of forms is evident.
But for one in whom both arising and passing away are discerned, the thought "my self arises and passes away" has occurred to them.
Therefore, it is not tenable for anyone to say, "Form is the self."
Thus, the eye is not-self, and forms are not-self.
For anyone who would say, "Eye-consciousness is self," that is not tenable.
For the arising and the passing away of eye-consciousness are discerned.
But for one in whom both arising and passing away are discerned, it occurs to him: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, it is not tenable for anyone to say: "Eye-consciousness is the self."
Thus, the eye is not-self, forms are not-self, and eye-consciousness is not-self.
If anyone were to say, "Eye-contact is the self," that would not be tenable.
For the arising and the passing away of eye-contact are discerned.
But for one in whom both arising and passing away are discerned, the thought "my self arises and passes away" has occurred to them.
Therefore, it is not tenable for anyone to say, "eye-contact is the self."
Thus, the eye is not-self, forms are not-self, eye-consciousness is not-self, and eye-contact is not-self.
If anyone were to say, "Feeling is self," that would not be tenable;
for in feeling, both arising and passing away are discerned.
But for one in whom both arising and passing away are perceived, it occurs to him: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, it is not tenable for anyone to say, "Feeling is the self."
Thus, the eye is not-self, forms are not-self, eye-consciousness is not-self, eye-contact is not-self, and feeling is not-self.
For anyone to say, "Craving is self," that is untenable;
for both the arising and the passing away of craving are discerned.
But for one in whom both arising and passing away are discerned, the thought occurs to him: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, it is not tenable for anyone to say: "Craving is the self."
Thus, the eye is not-self, forms are not-self, eye-consciousness is not-self, eye-contact is not-self, feeling is not-self, and craving is not-self.
Should anyone say, "The ear is self" ... [and so on] ...
should anyone say, "The nose is self" ... [and so on] ...
Whoever should say, ‘The tongue is the self’ …pe… whoever should say,
‘The body is the self’ …pe… whoever should say,
‘The mind is the self,’ that is not tenable.
The arising and passing away of mind is discerned.
For one in whom the arising and passing away are discerned, it occurs to them: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, that [notion] is not tenable:
‘The mind is self’—one who would say this [is wrong].
Thus, the mind is not-self.
‘Phenomena are self’—one who would say this is not tenable.
The arising and the passing away of phenomena are discerned.
For one for whom the arising and the passing away are discerned, the thought "my self arises and passes away" has occurred to them.
Therefore, that [position] is not tenable.
If anyone were to say, “Mental phenomena are the self,” [it would be so].
Thus, the mind is not-self, and mental phenomena are not-self.
If anyone were to say, “Mind-consciousness is the self,” that is untenable.
The arising and the passing away of mind-consciousness are discerned.
For one in whom the arising and the passing away are discerned, it follows that "my self arises and passes away.
Therefore, that [notion] is not tenable.
If someone were to say, ‘Mind-consciousness is the self,’ that is not tenable;
for thus, the mind is non-self, mental phenomena are non-self, and mind-consciousness is non-self.
If someone were to say, ‘Mind-contact is the self,’ that is not tenable.
The arising and the passing away of mind-contact are discerned.
For one in whom the arising and the passing away are discerned, it occurs to them: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, that [notion] is not tenable.
If anyone were to say, ‘Mind-contact is the self,’ it follows that the mind is not-self,
mental phenomena are not-self, mind-consciousness is not-self,
and mind-contact is not-self. If anyone were to say, ‘Feeling is the self,’ that is untenable.
The arising and the passing away of feeling are discerned.
For one in whom the arising and the passing away are discerned, it occurs to them: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, that [notion] is not tenable.
‘Feeling is self’— if one were to say this:
since the mind is not-self, mental phenomena are not-self, mind-consciousness is not-self, mind-contact is not-self, and feeling is not-self,
it would not be tenable for anyone to say, ‘Craving is self.’
The arising and the passing away of craving are discerned.
For one in whom the arising and the passing away are discerned, it occurs to them: "My self arises and passes away.
Therefore, that [notion of a self] is not tenable.
‘Craving is the self,’ one might say.
Thus, the mind is not-self, mental phenomena are not-self, mind-consciousness is not-self, mind-contact is not-self, feeling is not-self, and craving is not-self.
And this, monks, is the way leading to the origin of identity-formation:
One regards the eye as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
one regards forms as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
one regards eye-consciousness as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self.’
One regards eye-contact as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
one regards feeling as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
one regards craving as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self.’
One regards the ear as ‘this is mine, this I am,
this is my self’ … [and so on] … one regards the nose as ‘this is mine, this I am,
this is my self’ … [and so on] … one regards the tongue as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’ … [and so on].
One regards the body as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’ … [and so on] … one regards the mind as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
one regards mental phenomena as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
one regards mind-consciousness as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self.’
He regards mental contact as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
he regards feeling as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self’; he regards craving as ‘this is mine, this I am, this is my self.’
And this, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of identity:
one regards the eye thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
One regards forms thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
One regards eye-consciousness thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
One regards eye-contact thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
One regards feeling thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
One regards craving as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
One regards the ear as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"...
[and so on] ...one regards the nose as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"... [and so on].
One regards the tongue thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
... [and so on] ... one regards the body thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
... [and so on] ... one regards the mind thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
One regards mental phenomena thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
One regards mind-consciousness thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
One regards mind-contact thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
One regards feeling thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
One regards craving thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

And, monks, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, there arises a felt experience—either pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
When touched by a pleasant feeling, he delights in it, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it;
thus, the underlying tendency to lust lies latent within him.
When touched by a painful feeling, he sorrows, grieves, and laments; he weeps beating his breast and falls into confusion.
In him, the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent.

When touched by a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he does not understand, as it really is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding that feeling.
In him, the underlying tendency to ignorance lies latent.
"Indeed, monks, it is impossible that one who has not abandoned the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling, has not removed the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling,
and has not uprooted the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
one who has not abandoned ignorance and failed to arouse true knowledge— could make an end of suffering in this very life. Such a thing is not possible."
“Monks, dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises …pe… monks,
dependent on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises …pe… monks,
dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises …pe…”
“Monks, dependent on the body and tangible objects, body-consciousness arises... [as before] ...

Monks, dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there arises a feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Being touched by a pleasant feeling, one delights in it, welcomes it, and remains attached to it.”
The underlying tendency to lust lies latent within him.
When touched by a painful feeling, he sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, weeps, and falls into confusion;
the underlying tendency to aversion lies latent within him.
When touched by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not understand, as it truly is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding that feeling.
In him, the underlying tendency to ignorance lies latent.
Indeed, monks, for one who has not abandoned the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling and the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling...

Without having dispelled that [feeling], without having eradicated the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, without abandoning ignorance and giving rise to true knowledge, it is impossible for one to make an end of suffering in this very life.

For, monks, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there arises a feeling—either pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
When touched by a pleasant feeling, he does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it;
thus, the underlying tendency to lust does not lie within him.
When touched by a painful feeling, he does not grieve, does not lament, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.
The underlying tendency to aversion does not lie latent in him.
When touched by a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, he understands, as it really is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to that feeling.
The underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie latent in him.

“Indeed, monks, it is possible that one might abandon the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling, dispel the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling, and uproot the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
and having abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, one will make an end of suffering in this very life. This is possible.”
“Monks, dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises … [as before] … Monks,
dependent on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises … [as before] … Monks,
dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises … [as before] …”
“Dependent on the body and tangible objects, monks, body-consciousness arises...

[as before] ...Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, monks, mind-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there arises a feeling—either pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Being touched by a pleasant feeling, he does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.”
The underlying tendency to lust does not lie latent in him.
When touched by painful feeling, he does not grieve, does not waste away, does not lament, does not weep beating his breast, and does not fall into confusion.
The underlying tendency to aversion does not lie latent in him.
When touched by a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, one understands, as it truly is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding that feeling.
In such a person, the underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie latent.
Monks, having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling and the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling...
"Having dispelled it, having eradicated the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
having abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, he will make an end of suffering in this very life— this is possible. Seeing thus, bhikkhus,

the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, disenchanted with feeling, and disenchanted with craving."

One becomes disenchanted with the ear, one becomes disenchanted with sounds … [and so on] … one becomes disenchanted with the nose, one becomes disenchanted with odors … one becomes disenchanted with the tongue,
one becomes disenchanted with tastes …
One becomes disenchanted with the body; one becomes disenchanted with tangible objects...

one becomes disenchanted with the mind, disenchanted with mental phenomena, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, disenchanted with mind-contact, disenchanted with feeling, and disenchanted with craving.
Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,’ he understands.
This is what the Blessed One said.
With uplifted minds, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of about sixty bhikkhus were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
The Sixth Discourse on the Six Sets of Six is finished.
